The fourth: purified from being sent down upon the polytheists; this was said by al-Hasan.

It may also bear a fifth meaning: because it was sent down from a pure one, with pure ones, to a pure one.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 80, verses 17–32:**

﴿Death to man! How ungrateful he is!﴾ In ﴿Death to﴾ (*qutila*) there are two meanings:

First: he is punished.

Second: he is cursed.

Regarding ﴿man﴾ (*al-insan*) there are three opinions. First: it refers to every disbelIever. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: it refers to Umayyah ibn Khalaf. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: it refers to Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, when he said: "I have disbelieved in the Lord of the star when it sets." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, set Your dog upon him," and so a lion seized him on the road to Syria. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj and al-Kalbi.

Regarding ﴿how ungrateful he is!﴾ (*ma akfarahu*) there are three possible readings:

First: *ma* is an expression of wonder. It is the custom of the Arabs, when they marvel at something, to say: "May Allah fight him, how good he is!" and "May Allah disgrace him, how unjust he is!" The meaning is: marvel at the man's disbelief in light of all that we have mentioned after this.

Second: *ayyu shay'in akfarahu* ("what thing is it that makes him so ungrateful?"), in the form of a question. This is the view of al-Suddi and Yahya ibn Salam.

Third: *ma al'anahu* ("how accursed he is!"). This is the view of Qatadah.

﴿Then He made the way easy for him﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. First: his coming out from his mother's womb. This is the view of Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

Second: the way of happiness and misery. This is the view of Mujahid.

Third: the way of guidance and misguidance. This is the view of al-Hasan.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: the way of his benefits and harms.

﴿Then He caused him to die and assigned him a grave﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

First: He made him one who has a grave in which he is buried. This is the view of al-Tabari, who cited al-A'sha:

*"Were she to lean a dead man against her neck, he would live and would not be carried to a grave-digger."*

Second: He appointed someone to bury him and conceal him. This is the view of Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him﴾, meaning He will bring him back to life. Al-A'sha said:

*"Until people say, seeing what they see: 'How strange, the dead man being raised!'"*

﴿No! He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

First: it refers to the disbeliever, who has not done what he was commanded of obedience and faith. This is the view of Yahya ibn Salam.

Second: it is general, covering both the Muslim and the disbeliever. Mujahid said: "No one ever fulfills what has been obligated upon him." Here *kalla* is used to repeat the negation, and it is placed for refutation.

It is possible, in the sense of generality, that the disbeliever never fulfills it for his entire life, and the believer does not fulfill it for a month.

﴿Let man look at his food﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings:

First: at his food which he eats and by which his soul is sustained, of whatever kind it may be. This is the view of Yahya.

Second: at what comes out of him, of whatever kind it is, and then how it becomes, after the preservation of life and the death of the body.

Al-Hasan said: "An angel bends the neck of the son of Adam when he sits in the privy, to see what comes out of him."

The command to look may be understood in two ways:

First: so that he knows that he is a place of filth, and so does not become insolent.

Second: so that he may reason about the perishability of bodies, and so does not forget.

﴿That We pour down water abundantly﴾, meaning the rain.

﴿Then We split the earth open﴾, meaning with plants.

﴿And We cause grain to grow therein﴾, ﴿and grapes and fodder﴾. *Al-qadb* is fresh fodder and clover, named so because it is cut (*qadb*) after it has appeared.

﴿And olives and palm trees﴾, ﴿and dense gardens﴾. Concerning *ghulban* (dense) there are two opinions:

First: palm trees that are noble. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Second: tall and thick trees. al-Kalbi said: *al-ghulb* are the thick ones. al-Farazdaq said:

*"It howled and stirred up a thick-maned lion, so woe to the son of al-Maraghah for what he stirred up."*

Regarding *al-hada'iq* (gardens) there are three opinions: First: they are what is intertwined and gathered together. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Second: that it is the growth of all trees.

Third: that they are what is enclosed with palms and trees, and what is not enclosed is not a garden. This is related by Abu Salih.

It may also bear a fourth opinion: that *al-hada'iq* are those whose trees have matured, whose fruit has varied, until their goodness becomes general.

*Al-ghulb* may also mean those over which you have prevailed, yet they did not overpower you, and so were easy.

﴿And fruit and pasture﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions:

First: *al-abb* is what cattle graze upon. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. And what human beings eat is the harvested crop (*al-hasidah*). A poet, in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ), said:

*"His prayer is blessed, its wind is the east wind; by it Allah causes the harvest and the pasture to grow."*

Second: it is every plant that grows on the face of the earth. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: it is every plant other than fruit. This is the apparent view of al-Kalbi.

Fourth: it is fresh fruits. This is the view of Ibn Abi Talhah.

Fifth: it is specifically straw. This is also related from Ibn Abbas. A poet said:

*"For them there is no pasture for fodder, and the pasture among them is measured."*

I have found for some later scholars a sixth opinion: that fresh fruit is *fakihah*, and its dried form is *abb*.

It may also bear a seventh meaning: that *abb* is what does not reproduce like its root, such as grains, and *fakihah* is what does not reproduce like its root from trees.

It is narrated that Umar ibn al-Khattab recited ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, and when he reached His words, exalted is He, ﴿and fruit and pasture﴾, he said: "We know the fruit, but what is the *abb*?" Then he said: "By your life, O son of al-Khattab, this is indeed affectation," and he threw the staff from his hand.

This is an example which Allah, exalted is He, struck for the resurrection of the dead from their graves. They are like the plants of the crop after its decay, and it includes a reminder of the blessings which He has bestowed upon them.
